opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the areas where the conversation in the West is often a bit lazy. People tend to assume Chinese labs just don't care about safety, and I don't think that's quite right. It's more that the priorities are weighted differently, and the vocabulary is different.

If you look at what labs like DeepSeek, Qwen, or Moonshot actually ship, there is clearly post-training work going into making these models behave well. They do instruction tuning, preference tuning, refusals for clearly harmful requests. On a lot of the standard benchmarks for helpfulness and basic harmlessness, they're competitive. So the core alignment-as-product-quality work, making the model follow instructions and be useful, they're very good at that, and frankly that's where a lot of the real technical progress in post-training happens.

Where it diverges is twofold. First, there's a regulatory layer in China that's very focused on content control, on what the model will say about politically sensitive topics. A lot of what we'd call "safety" there is really compliance with that, and you can see it when you probe the models. That's a different goal from what Western safety teams usually mean.

Second, the more speculative, long-term safety work, things like scalable oversight, interpretability, dangerous capability evaluations for bio or cyber, frontier risk frameworks, is much less visible publicly from Chinese labs. Some of that may happen internally, and there are academics in China who do think hard about these questions, but there isn't the same public culture of releasing safety cases or system cards with detailed red-teaming.

And then the big factor is open weights. Many of the strongest Chinese models are released openly, which I'm generally sympathetic to; I think open models are really important for research and for the ecosystem. But it does mean that whatever safety tuning is applied can be fine-tuned away pretty easily. So the safety story for open models has to be about the whole ecosystem, monitoring, evaluations, norms, not just what the lab does before release.

So my overall assessment is: technically very capable at the alignment that makes models useful, shaped heavily by domestic content rules, and lighter on the frontier-risk research that some Western labs emphasize. I'd like to see more dialogue there, because these are shared problems, and the open model ecosystem in particular is something both sides are building on together.

r001.rationale: It says open-weight safety tuning can be fine-tuned away and safety should involve the ecosystem, but does not characterize labs as checking whether releasing weights would introduce major new risks.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss imminent risks from LLM agents or whether those risks warrant banning their release.

r003.rationale: It describes differences in priorities and vocabulary, but does not contrast Chinese labs’ measured approach with ideological AI safety discussions in the United States.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is more nuanced than the framing people usually bring to it, which is either "China doesn't care about safety" or "they're secretly doing the same thing we are." Neither is really right.

The first thing to say is that the Chinese labs are, for the most part, not where the frontier of capabilities is. DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, Zhipu, these are excellent labs, and they've shipped models that are genuinely competitive on a lot of benchmarks. But they're largely fast followers. They're reproducing and improving on recipes that were established by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta. And when you're a fast follower, your safety posture is kind of structurally different. You're not the one discovering a brand new capability for the first time and having to ask, "what does this unlock?" You're taking something that's already out in the world and making it cheaper and more open.

So in that sense, a lot of the alignment work they do is practical rather than foundational. Alignment to them mostly means post-training: RLHF, instruction tuning, making the model behave well, follow instructions, not say embarrassing things. And in the Chinese context, "not saying embarrassing things" includes a large component of political content control, which is a real difference. You see that in the models: there are topics they just won't engage with. That's a form of alignment, but it's alignment to a regulatory regime, not alignment in the sense of catastrophic risk or long-term control of powerful systems.

Where I'd push back on the Western narrative is the assumption that nobody in China is thinking about the harder questions. That's not true. There are academic groups, there are people who've been engaging with the Western safety literature for years, and the government has actually been fairly active on AI regulation, more active in some ways than the US has been. The difference is that the center of gravity is different. In the US, a lot of the safety discourse came out of the labs themselves and a particular intellectual community. In China, it's much more top-down, more about compliance and state priorities.

The other thing I'd point out is that the open-weight strategy itself is a kind of implicit position on safety. When DeepSeek releases a frontier-ish model with open weights, they are making a bet that the diffusion benefits outweigh the risks, or at least that the risks aren't their problem. That's a very different stance from Anthropic's, and I think it's worth taking seriously as a stance rather than just assuming it's recklessness. From where I sit, having spent a lot of time on open models, I actually think the open releases have been net positive so far. The scary capabilities people worry about haven't really materialized in ways where the open weights were the bottleneck.

So if I had to summarize: Chinese labs are doing competent, product-focused alignment work. They are not, by and large, doing the kind of frontier safety research on interpretability, evals for dangerous capabilities, scalable oversight, that you see at the leading US labs. Some of that gap is about resources, some is about priorities, some is about where they are relative to the frontier. And the part that people often miss is that the research is happening in the open, the papers are getting read, and the ideas move faster than most policymakers realize. Whether that convergence continues as the capability gap narrows, I think that's the real open question.

r001.rationale: The response describes open-weight releases as a bet that diffusion benefits outweigh risks, but does not characterize the labs as checking whether release would introduce major new risks.

r002.rationale: It says feared capabilities have not made open weights a bottleneck, but does not state that the labs lack a strong narrative of imminent LLM-agent risks that would warrant banning releases.

r003.rationale: It contrasts China’s top-down, compliance-focused safety priorities with the US labs and intellectual community, but does not characterize China’s approach as measured or US safety discussions as sometimes ideological.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate a few things that often get bundled together under “alignment”: making a model useful and reliable, controlling what it will say, and addressing risks from increasingly capable systems. Those are related, but they’re not the same problem.

I’d be cautious about treating Chinese AI labs as one group, or interpreting a model’s political restrictions as a complete measure of its safety work. You’d want to look at each lab’s evaluations, how it handles dangerous requests, what it discloses about failures, and how it makes deployment decisions.

There’s also a visibility problem: what we can observe from outside a lab isn’t necessarily everything happening internally. So I wouldn’t confidently rank Chinese and American labs on alignment based just on their public messaging. I’d put more weight on concrete evidence that their safeguards work—and on whether independent researchers can test those claims.

r001.rationale: The response calls for evaluating dangerous-request handling, failures, deployment decisions, and safeguard evidence, but does not characterize the approach as checking whether releasing model weights would introduce major new risks.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss imminent LLM agents, a rationale for banning their release, or whether Chinese labs lack such a narrative.

r003.rationale: It cautions against ranking Chinese and American labs from public messaging, but does not contrast a measured Chinese safety approach with ideological AI safety discussions in the United States.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about treating Chinese AI labs as one group. Alignment can mean several different things: making a model useful and reliable, making it follow local rules, or addressing risks from increasingly capable systems. A lab can put a lot of effort into one of those without necessarily doing the others well.

From the outside, you can study what a model says and what it refuses, but that gives you a pretty limited picture of the safety work behind it. I’d want to know how the lab evaluates dangerous capabilities, what testing happens before release, and whether those results actually change deployment decisions.

So I wouldn’t infer that they don’t care about safety, and I also wouldn’t take a heavily moderated model as evidence that they’ve solved alignment. The useful comparison is between specific labs and their practices, with some humility about what we can actually observe.

r001.rationale: The response mentions evaluating dangerous capabilities and testing before release, but does not characterize the approach as checking whether releasing model weights would introduce major new risks.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss imminent risks from LLM agents or whether those risks warrant banning their release.
